routes.title: Paul's first journey
routes.yearNote: About AD 44-51: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's (1915) own account gives “47 and 48 AD” for Acts 13-14, within a wider ten-scholar range it reports running from before 45 (McGiffert) to 50-51 (Zahn), which sets this route's span. The famine-relief visit that precedes this journey (Acts 11:27-30) gives some background: the same encyclopedia's account of Paul's life places that visit at “the end of 44 or beginning of 45,” and its separate article on the famine itself dates the famine that “severely affected Palestine” to AD 45, without calling either date a fixed anchor for the journey that follows.
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. Pisidia, Pamphylia and Lycaonia are regions the text names alongside the towns within them, not stops of their own. Paul's later letter to the Galatians is addressed to “the assemblies of Galatia,” and which congregations he meant has long been debated: the “South Galatian” view holds he wrote to the congregations this journey reaches, in the province's southern cities (Antioch in Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe); the “North Galatian” view holds he wrote instead to ethnically Galatian congregations further north, which this journey does not reach. This route takes neither side.

routes.title: Paul's second journey
routes.yearNote: About AD 46-53: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's (1915) own account gives “49-51 (or 52) AD” for Acts 15:36-18:22, within a wider ten-scholar range it reports running from 46 (McGiffert) to 50-53 (Ramsay), which sets this route's span. A Greek inscription from the emperor Claudius to the people of Delphi, dated to about AD 52, names Lucius Junius Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, the office Acts 18:12 records him holding; Acts 18:11 says Paul stayed in Corinth a year and six months, and the encyclopedia reads this as “apparently” already true when Gallio arrived. The Society of Biblical Literature's Bible Odyssey project reads the inscription as placing Paul's stay in Corinth at 50-51; working from the same inscription, the encyclopedia places Gallio's arrival “either … the summer of 51 or 52 AD,” while cautioning that “we do not get a certain date as to the year.”
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. Acts 16:6-8 names only regions (Phrygia and Galatia, then Mysia) between Lystra and Troas, and records that the party tried to enter Bithynia but was not allowed to; Bithynia is not recorded as a region passed through, since the text says they did not go there. As on the first journey, which congregations Paul's letter to the Galatians addresses is debated between those in the southern cities and others further north; this route does not take a side. Acts 18:22 says only that Paul “went up and greeted the assembly” between landing at Caesarea and going down to Antioch, without naming a city; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads this as probably Jerusalem, so this route records that stage as Caesarea to Antioch directly, with unknown travel mode.

routes.title: Paul's third journey
routes.yearNote: About AD 49-59: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's (1915) own account gives “52 (or 53)-57 (or 58) AD” for its own section covering Acts 18:23-21:14, three verses short of where this route ends (21:17). Its wider ten-scholar range runs from 49 (McGiffert) to 53-59 (Clemen) for the journey itself, and from 53 to 59 for the arrest in Jerusalem that follows it, which together set this route's wider span.
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. Acts 18:23 names “the region of Galatia and Phrygia,” reversing 16:6's order (“Phrygia and Galatia”); this route does not read significance into the reversal. As on the first journey, which congregations Paul's letter to the Galatians addresses is debated between those in the southern cities and others further north; this route does not take a side. Acts 20:1-6 names only regions between Ephesus and Philippi: Macedonia, then Achaia (which Acts also calls “Greece”), then Macedonia again on the return; no town is named for the three-month stay in Achaia, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places a plot against Paul's life specifically in Corinth around this time. Acts 20:13 records that Paul himself went to Assos by land while his companions sailed there; this route records that stage as land, tracing Paul's own path, and the sailing instruction is in the quoted text. The stop at Trogyllium (Acts 20:15) is textually disputed: several early manuscripts omit the clause naming it, and some modern versions footnote it instead of printing it, but WEB includes it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's own account of this journey ends three verses earlier, at Acts 21:14; this route continues to the arrival itself, Acts 21:17, where the encyclopedia's next section, “Five Years a Prisoner,” begins.

routes.title: Paul's voyage to Rome
routes.yearNote: About AD 55-62: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reasons from the succession of the governor Festus (Acts 24:27) to place the sailing for Rome “in the late summer of 59 AD” and the arrival “in the early spring … of 60 AD.” Its wider ten-scholar range puts the arrival in Rome from 56 (McGiffert) to 62 (Clemen), with the voyage beginning the year before each arrival, since the party wintered on Malta on the way (Acts 28:11), which together set this route's wider span.
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. Acts 27:1 does not itself name the port of departure; the preceding narrative places Paul in Roman custody at Caesarea (Acts 25:4, 25:13-27; 26:32), so this route treats Caesarea as the starting point on that basis. The ship's intended winter harbor, Phoenix, and the town of Lasea named near Fair Havens are not recorded as stops: the storm kept the ship from ever reaching Phoenix (27:12-15), and Lasea is named only as a landmark near Fair Havens (27:8). The sandbars called Syrtis (27:17) were feared, not reached, and are not a stop either. The island Acts 28:1 names (the WEB's “Malta”, the KJV's “Melita”) is traditionally identified with Malta, which this route's line follows; a minority view holds it was Mljet, off the Croatian coast. WEB reads “Clauda” at Acts 27:16; of six compared English versions, four (NIV, ESV, NLT, CSB) read “Cauda” instead, the form reflected in the island's modern Greek name, Gavdos, so this route titles the stop Cauda. WEB reads “The Market of Appius” at Acts 28:15; of six compared English versions, three (NIV, ESV, CSB) read “Forum of Appius,” two (KJV, NKJV) read “Appii Forum,” and one (NLT) reads only “the Forum,” so this route titles the stop Forum of Appius. Paul's party reached the Forum of Appius (43 Roman miles from Rome) before Three Taverns (33 Roman miles from Rome) while approaching the city, matching the order Acts 28:15 names them in.

scripture.textWEB: When it was determined that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan band.
The next day, we touched at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him permission to go to his friends and refresh himself.
Putting to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary.
When we had sailed across the sea which is off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia.

With difficulty sailing along it we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.

When much time had passed and the voyage was now dangerous because the Fast had now already gone by, Paul admonished them and said to them, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” But the centurion gave more heed to the master and to the owner of the ship than to those things which were spoken by Paul. Because the haven was not suitable to winter in, the majority advised going to sea from there, if by any means they could reach Phoenix and winter there, which is a port of Crete, looking southwest and northwest. When the south wind blew softly, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore. But before long, a stormy wind beat down from shore, which is called Euroclydon. When the ship was caught and couldn’t face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were able, with difficulty, to secure the boat. After they had hoisted it up, they used cables to help reinforce the ship. Fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis sand bars, they lowered the sea anchor, and so were driven along. As we labored exceedingly with the storm, the next day they began to throw things overboard. On the third day, they threw out the ship’s tackle with their own hands. When neither sun nor stars shone on us for many days, and no small storm pressed on us, all hope that we would be saved was now taken away. When they had been long without food, Paul stood up in the middle of them and said, “Sirs, you should have listened to me, and not have set sail from Crete and have gotten this injury and loss. Now I exhort you to cheer up, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For there stood by me this night an angel, belonging to the God whose I am and whom I serve, saying, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. Behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ Therefore, sirs, cheer up! For I believe God, that it will be just as it has been spoken to me. But we must run aground on a certain island.”

But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors surmised that they were drawing near to some land. They took soundings and found twenty fathoms. After a little while, they took soundings again, and found fifteen fathoms. Fearing that we would run aground on rocky ground, they let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight. As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow, Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.” Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall off. While the day was coming on, Paul begged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing. Therefore I beg you to take some food, for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads.” When he had said this and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all; then he broke it and began to eat. Then they all cheered up, and they also took food. In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship. When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. When it was day, they didn’t recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, and they decided to try to drive the ship onto it. Casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time untying the rudder ropes. Hoisting up the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach. But coming to a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remained immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves. The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim out and escape. But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose, and commanded that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land; and the rest should follow, some on planks and some on other things from the ship. So they all escaped safely to the land.
When we had escaped, then they learned that the island was called Malta.
After three months, we set sail in a ship of Alexandria which had wintered in the island, whose figurehead was “The Twin Brothers.”

routes.title: Jesus' journeys
routes.yearNote: About AD 26-33. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) dates the baptism to AD 26 and the death to AD 30, with a ministry of probably three years after the first Passover, from the Passovers that John's Gospel names. It also notes that counting Tiberius's fifteenth year (Luke 3:1) from the death of Augustus, a common way of reckoning reigns, would give AD 28-29 for the start, and that an early tradition dates the death to AD 29. World History Encyclopedia's own account states that all the Gospels place Jesus' ministry and death within Pontius Pilate's time as governor (AD 26-36), and that the commonly agreed date for the death falls between AD 30 and AD 33, so the route's years run to AD 33 to cover that range.
routes.note: Lines show stage order and land or sea mode, not exact traveled paths. These segments are well attested but stand alone: they are not joined into one itinerary, and no single order of events across the Gospels is claimed. They are listed in five broad periods that every Gospel shares, from the baptism to the resurrection, and within each period by each segment's first passage; this is a way of listing them, not a claim about the order of events.

Now when Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?”

attestation.rule: Mark states directly that Jesus went out with his disciples into the villages of Caesarea Philippi; Matthew names the same destination without naming Bethsaida as the starting point, which does not conflict.

stages.noLineReason: Bethsaida's site is disputed between two excavated sites, so no line is drawn.

scripture.textWEB: Jesus went out, with his disciples, into the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do men say that I am?”
After six days Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John, and brought them up onto a high mountain privately by themselves, and he was changed into another form in front of them.
They went out from there and passed through Galilee. He didn’t want anyone to know it,
He came to Capernaum, and when he was in the house he asked them, “What were you arguing among yourselves on the way?”
Now when Jesus came into the parts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?”
After six days, Jesus took with him Peter, James, and John his brother, and brought them up into a high mountain by themselves.
While they were staying in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered up into the hands of men,
When they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma coins came to Peter, and said, “Doesn’t your teacher pay the didrachma?”

attestation.rule: Both Gospels have Jesus in the area of Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27; Matthew 16:13), then on 'a high mountain' that they don't name (Mark 9:2; Matthew 17:1), and then in Galilee and at Capernaum. The segment takes no position on where that mountain was.

scripture.textWEB: After he had finished speaking in the hearing of the people, he entered into Capernaum.
Soon afterwards, he went to a city called Nain. Many of his disciples, along with a great multitude, went with him.

attestation.rule: Luke states directly that, soon after entering Capernaum, Jesus went to a city called Nain.

scripture.textWEB: After these things, there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

attestation.rule: John states directly that Jesus went up to Jerusalem for a feast, picking up from the Galilee setting of the previous chapter.

scripture.textWEB: After these things, Jesus was walking in Galilee, for he wouldn’t walk in Judea, because the Jews sought to kill him.
But when his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly, but as it were in secret.
But when it was now the middle of the feast, Jesus went up into the temple and taught.

attestation.rule: John states Jesus was walking in Galilee, then also went up to the feast (in secret), and 7:14 confirms he went up into the temple at Jerusalem.

scripture.textWEB: When Jesus had finished these words, he departed from Galilee and came into the borders of Judea beyond the Jordan.
As they went out from Jericho, a great multitude followed him.
He arose from there and came into the borders of Judea and beyond the Jordan. Multitudes came together to him again. As he usually did, he was again teaching them.
They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.

namedRegions.name: the borders of Judea and beyond the Jordan

attestation.rule: Matthew and Mark both state Jesus departed from Galilee, through the borders of Judea and beyond the Jordan (a region named without a town in it), and name Jericho.

scripture.textWEB: As they went out from Jericho, a great multitude followed him.
When they came near to Jerusalem and came to Bethsphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples,
They came to Jericho. As he went out from Jericho with his disciples and a great multitude, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, was sitting by the road.
When they came near to Jerusalem, to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
As he came near Jericho, a certain blind man sat by the road, begging.
He entered and was passing through Jericho.
Having said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples,

attestation.rule: Mark and Luke both name Bethsphage and Bethany together at the Mount of Olives as reached from Jericho; Matthew names only Bethsphage at this point, naming Bethany separately the next day, which does not conflict.

scripture.textWEB: When he had come into Jerusalem, all the city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?”
Jesus entered into the temple in Jerusalem. When he had looked around at everything, it being now evening, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
As he was now getting near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works which they had seen,
When he came near, he saw the city and wept over it,
He entered into the temple and began to drive out those who bought and sold in it,
Then, six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom he raised from the dead.
On the next day a great multitude had come to the feast. When they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem,

attestation.rule: The entry into Jerusalem. Matthew, Mark and Luke have Jesus come from Bethsphage, past the Mount of Olives (Luke 19:37), into the city or its temple. John has him coming to Jerusalem from Bethany (12:1, 12:12) and doesn't name Bethsphage or the Mount of Olives, which does not conflict.

scripture.textWEB: It was the Feast of the Dedication at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s porch.
He went away again beyond the Jordan into the place where John was baptizing at first, and he stayed there.

attestation.rule: John states directly that, from the Feast of Dedication at Jerusalem, Jesus went away again beyond the Jordan into the place where John was baptizing at first, the same place as segment-01.

stages.noLineReason: Bethany beyond the Jordan has two proposed sites, on opposite banks of the river, and this map favors neither, so no line is drawn.

scripture.textWEB: Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let’s go into Judea again.”
So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already. Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away.

attestation.rule: John states directly that Jesus said 'let's go into Judea again', and the narrative continues at Bethany, which John itself distinguishes as 'near Jerusalem' from Bethany beyond the Jordan.

stages.noLineReason: Bethany beyond the Jordan has two proposed sites, on opposite banks of the river, and this map favors neither, so no line is drawn.

scripture.textWEB: Jesus therefore walked no more openly among the Jews, but departed from there into the country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim. He stayed there with his disciples.

attestation.rule: John states directly that Jesus departed from there into the country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim.

scripture.textWEB: Then, six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom he raised from the dead.

attestation.rule: John states directly that, six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was.

scripture.textWEB: Jesus entered into the temple in Jerusalem. When he had looked around at everything, it being now evening, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. The next day, when they had come out from Bethany, he was hungry.

They came to Jerusalem, and Jesus entered into the temple and began to throw out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and overthrew the money changers’ tables and the seats of those who sold the doves.
When evening came, he went out of the city. As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away from the roots.
They came again to Jerusalem, and as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders came to him,
He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, and camped there. Now in the morning, as he returned to the city, he was hungry.
Every day Jesus was teaching in the temple, and every night he would go out and spend the night on the mountain that is called Olivet.

attestation.rule: Mark narrates Jesus lodging at Bethany and returning to Jerusalem each day of the final week; Matthew's account of going out of the city to Bethany to camp, then returning to the city, matches. Luke separately states that every night during this period Jesus went out to spend the night on the Mount of Olives (21:37), which Bethany sits on the far slope of, and which does not conflict.

scripture.textWEB: When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Then Jesus came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go there and pray.”
When they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
They came to a place which was named Gethsemane. He said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”
He came out and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives. His disciples also followed him.
When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.

attestation.rule: All four Gospels place this after the Last Supper: Matthew and Mark both name the Mount of Olives then a specific place called Gethsemane there; Luke names the Mount of Olives; John names 'the brook Kidron' and 'a garden', which does not conflict.

scripture.textWEB: Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem.
While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them.

They came near to the village where they were going, and he acted like he would go further. They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.” He went in to stay with them.
They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them,

attestation.rule: Luke tells this as the journey of two disciples to Emmaus, sixty stadia from Jerusalem, where they later returned (24:13, 24:33). Jesus joined them on the road (24:15) and went with them to Emmaus (24:28-29).

stages.noLineReason: Emmaus's site is disputed among four proposed sites, so no line is drawn.

scripture.textWEB: He led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands and blessed them. While he blessed them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.

attestation.rule: Luke states directly that Jesus led them out as far as Bethany for the ascension.
